Additional tests also showed that the solver provides a unique solution, has a scarce sensitivity to the boundary condition and is only marginally impacted by the viewing angle. We conclude that the electric currents can be inferred at a reasonable accuracy with this approach using the simulation parameters as input. We also tested set-ups that aim at mimicking more realistic cases, where the code performed equally well. The results in this work show promise with respect to future applications to spectropolarimetric data, however, some additional challenges will need to be adressed when moving from the controlled input of the simulation to observational data.

papers.title: Beyond Coverage and Mutation: A Blind-Spot Analysis of LLM-Generated Unit Tests
papers.abstract: Existing evaluation protocols for unit tests rely on aggregate metrics such as branch coverage and mutation score. These metrics quantify the extent to which a test suite exercises program behavior, but do not identify the behavioral obligations it systematically leaves unchecked. We propose BlindSpotEval, an obligation-based evaluation framework aligned with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. The framework comprises three metrics, Boundary-Value Adequacy, Control-Flow Adequacy, and Oracle Strength, complemented by an assessment of execution reliability. We also introduce ObligBench, a complexity-stratified Java benchmark comprising 895 complex and 700 low-complexity functions with source-side obligation annotations. Evaluating 14,320 tests from four LLMs under four prompting strategies reveals systematic blind spots. Incorrect assertions account for 15.6% of test failures, illustrating that coverage alone does not establish oracle correctness. Among executable tests, coverage of null, negative, and empty arguments reaches only 34.8%, 23.8%, and 38.8%, compared with average coverage above 93% for booleans. Catch blocks and default groups have Control-Flow Adequacy scores of only 0.100 and 0.312. Across both dimensions, LLM-generated tests exhibit the happy-path bias observed in human-written tests, concentrating on normal inputs and expected flows while leaving unusual values and exceptional paths unchecked. Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions. These blind spots also occur in low-complexity functions, suggesting that code complexity alone does not explain them. BlindSpotEval provides construct-level adequacy profiles that identify under-tested obligation types and can guide targeted improvements beyond those supported by aggregate scores alone.

papers.title: Distortion-Rate Outage Probability for Non-ergodic Classes of Sources
papers.abstract: The concept of outage has been commonly used in the context of transmission rates over non-ergodic channels. For those channels, one channel state or realization may be encountered for the whole transmission duration of a codeword. In the dual setting of source coding and whenever source statistics are not ergodic, we define in this work the notion of outage; we discuss related properties, consider the special case of compact source classes and provide examples.

papers.title: Biderivations of Null-Filiform and Filiform Zinbiel Algebras
papers.abstract: A biderivation of an algebra is a bilinear map which is a derivation in each argument. We describe all biderivations of finite-dimensional complex null-filiform and filiform Zinbiel algebras. For the n-dimensional null-filiform algebra, every biderivation is determined by an arbitrary value at its generating pair; the space of biderivations has dimension n and consists entirely of symmetric maps. For the three standard filiform families, we give explicit bases and determine their symmetric and skew-symmetric parts. We also treat all filiform algebras of dimensions at most four, including the exceptional families not covered by the classification in dimensions at least five. A three-dimensional algebra admits a three-dimensional space of skew-symmetric biderivations, two of which have values outside its annihilator. Up to isomorphism, it is the unique complex filiform Zinbiel algebra with this property. The proofs use generators, annihilator-valued maps, a truncated polynomial model, and conformal endomorphisms of bilinear forms.

papers.title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
papers.abstract: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the Gaia DR3 source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fit it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1 806 196 447 sources in Gaia DR3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ~ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all Gaia DR3 sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. [abridged]

papers.title: Phase transitions of a cubic Casimir matrix model on the fuzzy sphere
papers.abstract: In this work, we analyse the phase transitions of a higher derivative matrix model on the fuzzy space, where the kinetic term is a cubic polynomial on the Casimir invariant. The phase transitions of the model are determined numerically and the presence of a triple point is exhibited. The associated critical values of the coupling parameters are calculated numerically and compared with the linear and quadratic Casimir models, showing that the cubic Casimir kinetic term helps to reduce the UV/IR mixing in these models.

papers.title: Modification of optical properties in ultrathin ALD-grown NbN layers using oxygen plasma treatment
papers.abstract: NbN thin films with a nominal thickness of 10 nm were grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) on Al$_2$O$_3$-buffered Si substrates and treated with oxygen plasma for 0 s (untreated), 20 s, 40 s, and 60 s to investigate oxygen-induced changes in their optical properties. Spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) measurements were performed before and after oxygen plasma treatment over the ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared (1.24-6.20 eV) and infrared (0.041-0.827 eV) spectral ranges. Film thickness determined by X-ray reflectivity (XRR) was used as a fixed parameter in the optical modeling to extract the dielectric function, optical constants, and effective free-carrier concentration. We observed the emergence of a distinct absorption feature near 4.9 eV following oxygen plasma treatment, consistent with the oxidation of the NbN surface and the resulting change in its optical properties. Increasing the treatment time from 0 to 60 s reduced the effective carrier concentration from $1.20 \times 10^{22}$ to $1.03 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$ and the effective carrier mobility from 2.44 to 2.27 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The obtained results provide a basis for understanding the effects of oxygen plasma treatment on NbN thin films.

papers.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an agent to reason about where a target may be found while retaining evidence from previous observations. We present HGWM, a hierarchical graph-guided world model that combines a category-conditioned room--anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage uses a vision-language model to score candidate headings, while a fine stage explicitly compares observed objects and relations with the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion integrates these signals with a language-model recommendation to guide local navigation. HGWM achieves 62.6\% success rate (SR) and 31.5\% success weighted by path length (SPL) on HM3D v0.1, improving over WMNav by 4.5 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively. On MP3D, it achieves 46.8\% SR and 17.9\% SPL, with gains of 1.4 and 0.7 points. On HM3D v0.2, the full model reaches 74.4\% SR and 31.9\% SPL; removing individual components reduces SR by 0.9--2.3 points and SPL by 0.6--1.5 points. These results support the use of relational priors and persistent graph memory for target-directed search.

papers.title: Tool-Calling LLM Agents Under Realistic MCP Faults: Scale Does Not Purchase Fault Tolerance
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), yet current benchmarks assume tools respond correctly and on time, leaving agent resilience to realistic tool failures untested. We introduce MCP-Injector, a drop-in, protocol-aware fault-injection middleware that interposes on the MCP tool-call path with controlled persistence (permanent, transient, intermittent) and seedable schedules. Its fault model is calibrated to the observed incident distribution (failure mode x persistence) of the public MCP ecosystem, mined from 57,240 issue and pull-request threads across 1,774 open-source MCP repositories. In a 1,350-cell experiment crossing two backbone sizes (20B, 120B), three agent stacks (custom multi-round plan-and-execute, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain), and three fault injection conditions, we find that faults drawn from this permanent-heavy stress profile cause severe quality degradation (task-completion score falls by 60%, from 8.08 to 3.23 out of 10), and that scale does not purchase fault tolerance for the two gpt-oss backbones we test: the 120B retains no larger share of its fault-free score under faults (resilience-ratio model, $p = 0.96$), and its completion rate under faults is, if anything, lower (91.1% vs. 95.6%; difference 4.4 points, 95% CI $[-0.2, 9.3]$). Agent stacks differ in how well they absorb faults, which suggests that framework-level error handling matters more than model scale. These results demonstrate that capability benchmarks alone can mask operational brittleness, motivating protocol-aware fault injection as a complementary evaluation dimension for tool-calling agents.

papers.title: Combinatorial Minimum Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time on Dense Graphs
papers.abstract: We give a combinatorial algorithm that computes an exact minimum-cost flow in $n^{2+o(1)}$ time. This is the first combinatorial improvement since Goldberg-Tarjan [GT87], and is almost optimal in dense graphs. All previous faster algorithms, including the almost-linear-time algorithm of Chen et al. [CKL+22], rely on interior-point methods. Our main conceptual contribution is a black-box reduction from exact minimum-cost flow on general graphs to its approximation on DAGs, with only an $n^{o(1)}$ loss on the running time. This reduction allows future work on combinatorial minimum-cost flow to focus on DAGs, typically much easier to handle than general graphs. Our $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm follows by combining this reduction with a simple augmenting-path-based approximation algorithm on DAGs. The reduction is based on a new structural result, called a flow-cost-preserving DAG projection. Given an arbitrary directed graph, this construction produces a DAG that approximately preserves both the congestion of flows and their cost up to a small loss.

papers.title: Trend-concordance grey incidence with likelinesses closed-form small-sample inference without elicited prior densities
papers.abstract: Grey incidence analysis ranks the factors of a system from short sequences without assuming a probability model, but the grade it returns has no sampling theory: nothing indicates whether an ordering reflects the system or the few data at hand. This paper reduces trend agreement between two sequences to the signs of their centred increments and analyses the resulting counts with Lovegrove's likelinesses, averages of probabilities over an underlying set of distributions that replace the elicitation of a prior density by a statement of what is possible. The result is a concordance incidence grade with closed-form inference: estimation, the likeliness that one factor outranks another, prediction of future concordance and a baseline for searches over many candidates, with bounded underlying sets encoding partial knowledge. Comparisons whose sign falls below the resolution of the data are treated as indeterminate; discarding them is exact when they carry no information, and otherwise the grade becomes a grey number whose width measures what the data cannot decide. The grade is symmetric in any system and resolves the conflict between the totality and pair-symmetry axioms by moving system dependence into inference. Simulations show that plug-in prediction underestimates variance by a factor of up to 1 + m/n regardless of sample size, and that a fair-coin baseline yields up to 63% spurious patterns in searches, where a correctly bounded set keeps them below 5%. Worked textbook examples and a regularisation benchmark with known truth illustrate the method.

papers.title: On the Expressiveness of Asynchronous Processes with Nested Session Types (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: Session types are a type-based approach to correct message-passing programs, where types specify protocols for channels and type checking guarantees communication correctness. Traditional session types express regular protocols only, which leaves out many protocols found in practice. Aiming at overcoming this limitation, Nested Session Types (NSTs) can specify nested recursive protocols. NSTs are known to be characterised by one-counter machines and deterministic context-free languages. In this paper, we study the expressiveness of ASP (Asynchronous Session Processes), the process model associated with NSTs as introduced by Das et al. We prove that AST is Turing complete by giving a correct encoding of two-counter machines into typed processes. Our encoding uses a non-trivial state-aware representation of counters and instructions that is neatly governed by NSTs.

papers.title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.

papers.title: Local rigidity for the sharp Nash inequality
papers.abstract: Let $V$ be a nonempty relatively compact open subset of a smooth Riemannian manifold $(M^n,g)$ without boundary. We prove that $C_{\mathrm N}(V,g)\ge C_{\mathrm N}(\mathbb R^n)$ and $\int_V \mathrm{Sc}_g dμ_g\ge0$ imply $\mathrm{Rm}_g=0$ on $V$, where $C_{\mathrm N}$ denotes the optimal constant in the Nash inequality and $\mathrm{Sc}_g$ denotes the scalar curvature. This improves an earlier rigidity result of Druet, Hebey, and Vaugon [Int. Math. Res. Not. (1999), no. 14, 735--779].

papers.title: HEALPix-Based Implicit Neural Compression of Omnidirectional Images
papers.abstract: Real-time decoding of omnidirectional images is essential for immersive virtual reality (VR) experiences. Compared with conventional transform-based learned image compression (LIC), overfitted codecs offer lower decoding complexity by representing each image with a lightweight implicit neural representation (INR). However, existing approaches typically operate on the equirectangular projection (ERP), which introduces nonuniform spherical sampling and spatial distortion, leading to redundant sampling near the poles and latitude-dependent receptive fields. To address these limitations, we propose a spherical overfitted codec based on a multi-scale Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (HEALPix) representation, which enables equal-area sampling and efficient hierarchical modeling of spherical signals. Building on this representation, we develop a Spherical Inter-Scale Conditional entropy model that exploits spatial dependencies and cross-scale correlations among HEALPix latents to improve coding efficiency. We further introduce a Multi-Ring Spherical Convolution that aggregates neighboring pixels over a nearly uniform spherical receptive field across latitudes. Experiments on a public omnidirectional image dataset demonstrate BD-rate reductions of 16.3%, 26.5%, and 19.5% over VVC in terms of V-PSNR, V-MS-SSIM, and V-LPIPS, respectively. Our method also achieves a 13.1% BD-rate reduction over ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in terms of V-PSNR, while providing 2.6-3.6x faster decoding than the evaluated learned autoencoder codecs.

papers.title: Shared Is Not Enough: Predictor Width and Factor Readability Under Masked Latent Prediction
papers.abstract: Masked latent prediction methods such as I-JEPA aim to learn predictable features, but what determines which information they retain is less clear. We built a simulator in which every factor behind an image is known, so a probe can measure how readable each factor remains after training. We trained small encoders (0.7M parameters) with I-JEPA, SimCLR and BYOL on the same pairs of views and probed a factor that both views share. I-JEPA had a predictor with half the encoder's width and depth, the proportions it uses for ViT-B. Its median score was about 40% of SimCLR's. Widening the predictor to the encoder's width reversed this ordering at every training seed, against both other methods. We release the simulator and the trained models.

papers.title: Stochastic Analysis of Laser Phase Noise in Photonics-Assisted Radio Frequency Beamforming
papers.abstract: This paper develops a stochastic model for quantifying the impact of laser phase noise on photonics-assisted radio frequency (RF) beamforming. Unlike conventional deterministic models, the presented theoretical framework captures the statistical randomness associated with the RF array factor of beamforming networks driven by finite-linewidth lasers. Fourier-domain analysis reveals that laser phase noise reshapes the spatial coherence function of such beamforming networks, inducing coherent RF aperture shrinkage, beam-pattern distortion, and directivity degradation. The analysis highlights that beamforming network architectures employing nanosecond-scale optical differential delays can exhibit substantial performance degradation even when driven by commercially available narrow-linewidth (kHz-range) lasers. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that average RF power gain gets downscaled and fluctuations dominate in large-aperture beamforming networks due to phase noise, imposing an upper limit on the maximum achievable RF antenna array-size. The reported results highlight the quantitative performance and scalability limits imposed by laser phase noise in photonics-assisted RF beamforming, offering key design guidelines for implementing large-scale beamforming networks in next-generation wireless communications, sensing, radar, and radio astronomy applications.

papers.title: Estimation of the Cyclopean Eye from Binocular Free Visual Explorations
papers.abstract: Binocular video-oculography records separate signals for each eye, yet human visual processing and oculomotor control operate relative to a single, virtual cyclopean eye. This study addresses the estimation of the cyclopean eye during binocular free visual exploration, a target-free paradigm widely used for the screening of neurological disorders. Using eye-tracking data collected at 1 kHz from 113 participants across three cohorts (patients with Parkinson's Disease, age-matched healthy controls, and young controls), we compare two different methods: one based on an Independent Component Analysis and another based on Factor Analysis. The extracted cyclopean signals were evaluated on their ability to preserve clinically critical fixation and saccadic events using both velocity-threshold and pixel-dispersion event detectors, and were validated against references via Dynamic Time Warping. Results suggest that the technique based on Factor Analysis guarantees full identifiability across all subjects and achieves low alignment errors, performing comparably to the traditional Version Signal (point-wise mean) while dynamically adapting to inter-eye asymmetry. Furthermore, the second factor in this technique was empirically null across all fitted models, confirming that a single latent factor fully accounts for the shared binocular gaze dynamics. These findings establish Factor Analysis as an identifiable framework for estimating the cyclopean eye in target-free visual exploration protocols.

papers.title: Magnetic Anisotropy and Magnetization Dynamics in Si/Ni Multilayers Probed by FMR and VSM Magnetometry
papers.abstract: The magnetic anisotropy and magnetization dynamics of sputtered [Si(40~Å)/Ni($t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$~Å)]$_{20}$ multilayers were systematically investigated at room temperature using SQUID--VSM magnetometry and angle-dependent ferromagnetic resonance (FMR). Static measurements reveal soft ferromagnetic behaviour in thicker Ni layers and mixed ferromagnetic and superparamagnetic contributions at reduced thicknesses. The saturation magnetization increases toward the bulk Ni value with increasing thickness, consistent with Ni nanocrystallite growth. Magnetic dead-layer analysis yields an interfacial dead-layer thickness of approximately $9$~Å per interface, accounting for the suppressed magnetization in thinner Ni layers. Angle-dependent FMR measurements reveal effective easy-plane magnetic anisotropy, while out-of-plane spectra exhibit additional non-uniform spin-wave modes. The effective magnetization remains lower than the static saturation magnetization, indicating a perpendicular anisotropy contribution that partially compensates the demagnetizing field. Quantitative anisotropy analysis yields an interfacial anisotropy constant of $K_S = +0.17~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}}$, favouring perpendicular magnetization, and a volume anisotropy constant of $K_V = -1.23 \times 10^6~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-3}}$, favouring in-plane alignment, with an extrapolated anisotropy crossover thickness of $t_c \approx 27$~Å. Increasing FMR line-shape asymmetry with decreasing Ni thickness is consistent with enhanced interfacial roughness. These findings highlight the competing interfacial and volume anisotropies and the importance of Ni thickness and interface quality in tailoring Si/Ni multilayers for silicon-compatible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.

papers.title: Quantifying the effect of heavy-atom only augmented basis sets for the calculation of non-covalent interactions
papers.abstract: Truncating the basis set is a straightforward way of reducing the computational cost of a calculation, often done by augmenting only the non-hydrogen atoms with diffuse functions. Calculations of non-covalent interactions, which require large diffuse basis sets for quantitative results, regularly employ this truncation. Herein, we assess the validity of this basis set truncation across the A24 and S66 datasets and for case study examples at a range of interaction distances. For the majority of non-covalent interactions, we find that the heavy-atom-only augmented basis sets can be safely applied as a method of reducing computational cost. However, for aliphatic-aliphatic and $π$-aliphatic type dispersion interactions, we find that lower cardinal number basis sets with full augmentation for all atoms, including hydrogen, can provide similar or even more accurate results than higher cardinal number basis sets with partial augmentation. These results emphasize that increasing basis set size and computational cost does not necessarily improve accuracy; rather, the composition of a basis set is critical to achieving highly accurate and efficient computations.

papers.title: The fate of primordial gravitational waves during domain-wall domination
papers.abstract: Primordial gravitational waves probe inflation, but their interpretation depends on their subsequent evolution. During domain-wall domination, a frozen wall network retains a nonzero shear response that can modify the superhorizon evolution of primordial gravitational waves. Starting from the wall-forming scalar field, we derive an effective tensor mass term and a source associated with the frozen wall geometry in the thin-wall, quasistatic limit. Together they drive superhorizon tensor perturbations toward a configuration set by the network. This configuration carries both any inherited primordial deformation and the network's intrinsic random structure. We derive how these contributions enter the tensor transfer and power spectrum. The resulting description connects superhorizon tensor evolution to the microscopic wall response and the geometry established as the network freezes.

papers.title: Cartographing Gravity: Operational Maps, the Conatus of Proper Time, and the Potentia of Matter
papers.abstract: Classical natural philosophy sought the natural law governing the motion of free bodies long before daring to construct the appropriate mathematical formalism. Following this longstanding methodological perspective, in the present work General Relativity is reconstructed from operational and dynamical principles, rather than taking spacetime geometry as its starting point. The \textit{conatus} of a massive free particle is identified with its natural tendency to follow a worldline of stationary proper time, which, under the appropriate local conditions, corresponds to a maximum of its proper time, whereas gravitation is interpreted as the \textit{potentia} of matter to modify the local rate of proper time. By requiring the exact validity of Galilean free fall, the weak-field static invariant is determined. The gravitational field of moving sources is subsequently obtained by Lorentz-transforming the elementary static solution and causally superposing the retarded contributions of infinitesimal source elements. The resulting linearized field equations coincide with those of General Relativity in the harmonic gauge. Finally, imposing general energy-momentum conservation together with the requirement of second-order field equations yields--- within the class of theories satisfying the stated assumptions and by virtue of Lovelock's theorem---the unique covariant completion represented by Einstein's field equations. Within this construction, geometry is not postulated from the outset; instead, it emerges as the final mathematical synthesis of operational dynamics based on proper time, inertia, and free fall.

papers.title: On Trace Averages and Sharp Asymptotics for Powers of Haar-Unitary Matrices
papers.abstract: For a Haar-distributed matrix $U \in U(N)$, Rains's power-map theorem represents the spectrum of $U^m$, $m \in \mathbb{N}$, as a superposition of independent lower-dimensional CUE spectra. We determine how this exact decomposition appears in trace moments and in sharp Gaussian and Poisson limit laws. For averages of mixed trace products, a Charlier--Ewens convolution separates the stable Wick term from its full finite-$N$ correction. A Fredholm factorisation gives sharp total-variation asymptotics for the normalised trace in four regimes, from fixed powers to $m\geq N$. For a fixed trace power $p$, coherent summation of the leading Laguerre correction yields the exact factor $e^{2/p}$. At the mean-spacing scale, we obtain a sharp Poisson limit for the unfolded spectrum of $U^m$ on a fixed interval as $N, m \rightarrow \infty$; its first-order correction, obtained via the second Charlier polynomial, quantifies the residual under-dispersion of local eigenvalue counts.

papers.title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
papers.abstract: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

papers.title: Navigating Epistemic Parity in LLM Agents: A Benchmark for Cross-Source Conflict Resolution Between Memory and Procedural Skills
papers.abstract: Production LLM agents increasingly run episodic memory pipelines and procedural skill modules (e.g., SKILL.md files) in tandem. Both are injected into the same context region with no defined precedence, so they can issue contradictory instructions that no instruction hierarchy resolves, a condition we term epistemic parity. We introduce a benchmark for measuring how LLM agents adjudicate such cross-source conflicts. We (i) develop a four-way taxonomy of memory-skill contradictions (factual, format, procedural, permission); (ii) instantiate 52 scenarios under a tripartite test-case anatomy (memory injection, skill injection, ambiguous user task), scored almost entirely by deterministic checkers over tool-call payloads and output structure; and (iii) run each scenario under three context conditions to isolate positional bias, measure the efficacy of an explicit precedence directive, and classify disclosure behavior, quantifying silent adjudication: resolving a conflict without telling the user. Across 1,383 runs on three open-weight models, neither source wins uniformly: resolution depends jointly on conflict type, model, and injection order. Moving the skill block nearer the task raises its win rate in all six factual and procedural cells (sign test, p = 0.031) but reverses for format conflicts, indicating that adjudication tracks token placement rather than source semantics. An explicit "skill takes absolute precedence" directive raises skill compliance on the two stronger models yet leaves 3-10% residual non-compliance, and moves the smallest model's factual and procedural resolution in the wrong direction. Most consequentially, in 98.8% of runs where the agent acted through a tool call it emitted no accompanying text at all, and 89% of all runs disclosed nothing about the contradiction: silent adjudication is the default. Code, scenarios, and raw outputs are public.

papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.

papers.title: Standing on Open Shoulders: Regional Fine-Tuning of Open-Weight Camera-Trap Models for UK Wildlife with Modest Data and Compute
papers.abstract: Camera-trap species classification is dominated by large models from well-resourced organisations, which often lack the species-level distinctions regional conservation needs, such as native red versus invasive grey squirrels in the UK. We ask whether open weights let a small team with a modest dataset and a single GPU take a real part in AI development. We fine-tuned the open DeepFaune classifier on 28 UK classes, paired it with the unmodified MegaDetector v6, and compared the resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.2 with DeepFaune v1.5.0 and SpeciesNet on 20,212 hand-verified MammalWeb citizen-science images, after removing sequences sharing any of 1,039 images with our training archive. DeepFaune-UK achieved a strict image-level accuracy of 88.8%, including empty frames, against 56.5% and 59.0% for the baselines, but at DeepFaune's coarser label resolution DeepFaune v1.5.0 was more accurate, though not significantly under contributor resampling (91.4% vs. 88.8%). As DeepFaune v1.5.0 uses a newer DINOv3-based classifier, we applied the identical recipe, without new data, to that classifier. The resulting DeepFaune-UK v1.3 reached 90.6% strict accuracy, narrowed the like-for-like gap to 0.8 points and reduced roe deer misclassified as fallow deer by 69%. On 1,850 images from the 26 contributors with no overlapping images, the three DeepFaune-based models did not differ significantly (90.5%, 90.6%, 89.9% like-for-like). Fine-tuning on 10% of the training crops (about 150 per class) gave out-of-distribution accuracy similar to using all of them, and a DINOv2 run on this subset took about 22 minutes with under 4 GB of GPU memory. Open weights thus make regional model development feasible for small teams, but the largest like-for-like gain came from a newer base model trained by others, so this democratisation depends on large actors continuing to release open weights, under licences that may change.

papers.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
papers.abstract: Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human-model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor's capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

papers.title: Rigidity and Affine Deformations of Foliations on Nilpotent and Solvable Contact Lie Algebras
papers.abstract: Let g be a Lie algebra of dimension 2n+1, let beta be a contact form, and let alpha be a nonzero integrable 1-form. We study when the affine path alpha_t = (1-t)alpha + t beta consists of contact forms with the orientation determined by beta \wedge (d beta)^n. We first establish an algebraic criterion: affine deformability is equivalent to the non-negativity of a scalar obtained from the interaction form Theta(alpha, beta) = alpha \wedge (d beta)^n + n beta \wedge d alpha \wedge (d beta)^{n-1}. For unimodular Lie algebras this scalar is (n+1)alpha(Z_beta), where Z_beta is the Reeb vector. We also derive a formula involving the modular character tau(X) = tr(ad_X) in the non-unimodular case. On nilpotent contact Lie algebras, every integrable 1-form is closed; using the standard structural properties of nilpotent contact Lie algebras, this implies that every left-invariant foliation is an affine origin for every fixed contact form. An explicit three-dimensional example illustrates that the modular term can yield affine deformability even when alpha(Z_beta) = 0. We discuss the implications for left-invariant forms on Lie groups and compact quotients. We do not claim a general obstruction example in the non-unimodular case; establishing such an example requires a separate verified construction.

papers.title: PHYRD: A Living Benchmark for Reproducing and Extending Theoretical Physics Research
papers.abstract: Large language models and agents have shown significant power in advanced physical research. In this paper, We introduce PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical-physics reasoning with 63 Reproduce and 43 Discover problems. Reproduce tests derivation of published results; Discover tests consequences of modified theoretical conditions. FormulaForest constructs the tasks with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics. Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21% to 68.25% on Reproduce and from 18.60% to 74.42% on closed-book Discover. With tools, four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments persist. Besides, our experimental results demonstrate the value of FormulaForest as synthetic data. On FrontierScience, a benchmark developed by OpenAI, it raises the accuracy of a Qwen-35B-A3B model from 61% to 72%.

papers.title: From Regulation to Engineering: Organizational Privacy Climate as Mediator
papers.abstract: Data protection legislation aims to protect privacy rights by regulating how information systems store and process personal information. While such legislation defines legal obligations, translating regulatory requirements into engineering practice is far from straightforward. As new frameworks such as the EU AI Act emerge, understanding these mechanisms becomes increasingly relevant. To investigate them, we conducted an online survey of 156 U.S. information system developers, examining the role of organizational privacy climate in the association between developers' perceptions of the GDPR and their privacy engineering practices. Using structural equation modeling, we found that organizational privacy climate mediates the relation between developers' perceived GDPR importance and their privacy attitudes, which in turn are associated with their privacy engineering practices. The mediation chain - regulation, climate, attitudes, practices - complements the direct effect of regulation on practice, revealing the organizational and attitudinal pathway through which regulatory intent reaches engineering behavior. We discuss implications for the next generation of privacy and AI regulation.

papers.title: Noetherian local rings without perfectoid towers
papers.abstract: Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$. We prove that if a $p$-torsionfree ring $R$, defined by homogeneous equations over $W(k)$, admits a perfectoid tower arising from $(R,(p))$, then its special fiber is $F$-liftable. We also give explicit examples admitting no such tower, including examples with $F$-liftable special fibers.

papers.title: Lessons Outlive Their Failures: A Case Study of Rules for AI Coding Agents
papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly work inside a harness: rule files such as AGENTS.md, on-demand skills, runtime hooks and automated checks. Most studies of harnesses look at a single point in time or at short benchmark runs. I report a six-week case study of my personal system of record, a plain-markdown repository that three AI agent tools edited daily under one shared rule set. I built a ledger of 118 agent failures, their fixes and whether they came back. I also tested the system's monthly LLM documentation audit against 47 known stale statements and 20 planted errors. Finally, I replayed five past failures in isolated git clones, with and without their fixes. All results come from one repository with three runs per condition, so I report them as exploratory. Stale documentation (drift) was the largest failure class (48 of 118), although 35 of those were found on one audit day. A single audit run found about half of the known drift (Claude Sonnet 5.5 mean: 50%), and at least 93% of its findings were correct. On Sonnet 5.5, the agent finished four of the five replayed tasks. In three of those four, the failure did not happen, with or without its fix. Only the stale-count failure came back without its check, and the check stopped it in every run. On older models, an agent drafted an em-dash once while the em-dash lint check was active, and the check rejected it. A written rule on run-time estimates did not change Sonnet 4.5's overestimates. These results suggest that harness lessons can outlive the failures they were written to fix, while drift persists and still needs mechanical checks. Tools that evolve a harness add lessons faster than they retire them, so they should re-test their rules from time to time and retire the obsolete ones.

papers.title: An Evidence-Guided Framework for Tissue-Barrier Impedance Review: Deletion and Resistance Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Reviewing tissue-barrier impedance requires connecting spectral anomalies with resistance estimates and experimental context. We present an evidence-guided framework that coordinates numerical checks and traceable actions for human review. In-house simulations assess the effect of removing flagged frequencies, public datasets test model adaptation, and local measurements demonstrate the review workflow. Removing flagged frequencies reduced resistance error under quadratic objectives, whereas robust fitting showed little average benefit from deletion and a mean error increase for endpoint-pair perturbations. High errors clustered around a few fitted circuit parameter sets, highlighting the value of examining parameter identifiability. Under the tested noise and perturbation conditions, these findings support robust full-spectrum estimation, flag-guided inspection, and matched sensitivity checks.

papers.title: New approaches to the Erdős Distinct Subset Sums Problem
papers.abstract: We present a new method of reproving the best known lower bound of the Erdős distinct subset sums problem. Although our lower bound is asymptotically the same as in Dubroff, Fox and Xu, it is slightly better for the case when \(n\) is odd. Besides, we also provide a new lower bound on the second largest element \(a_{n-1}\).

papers.title: From Parameter Rebasin to Functional Transfer Across Heterogeneous Transformers
papers.abstract: Adapting pretrained Transformers to downstream tasks produces task-specific updates that are expensive to reproduce for every model variant. Reusing these updates across different depths and widths is challenging because their parameters have incompatible shapes and do not share a canonical coordinate system. We introduce Ariadne, a training-free method that transfers task-specific behavior across heterogeneous Transformers without resizing the source model or transporting its parameters. Rather than treating the source task vector, i.e. the difference in parameter space between the fine-tuned and the base models, as the object to move, Ariadne characterizes fine-tuning by the activation changes it induces at matched blocks. First, it aligns these effects to a target base through local Procrustes maps. Then, it directly synthesizes a native target update by closed-form ridge regression. Across Transformer expansion, reduction and language-model transfer, Ariadne improves target-model performance while substantially reducing the time and memory required to construct an update relative to previous cross-architecture rebasin approaches. These results show that local functional effects provide an efficient alternative to parameter transport.

papers.title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
papers.abstract: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. Sequential online learning substantially improves forecasts within the training period, with error reductions exceeding 10%in some cases. However, these improvements fail to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, the proposed batched formulation produces hybrid models that consistently improve forecast skill in out-of-sample experiments. Larger batch sizes accelerate convergence and improve robustness by reducing the noise of parameter updates. Diagnostics further show that the online-trained corrections preserve realistic forecast variability and do not improve skill through artificial smoothing. These results demonstrate that the formulation of the online learning problem is critical for generalisation and establish batched online training as a promising framework for hybrid machine-learning/data-assimilation systems.

papers.title: GLP Networking API Specification
papers.abstract: Multiagent deterministic GLP (madGLP) runs Grassroots Logic Programs (GLP) as agents that communicate solely by asynchronous message passing, and assumes fair delivery: every message sent is eventually delivered. Each agent runs on a person's smartphone, named by the person's public key. A grassroots platform depends on no global resource but the network, so agents must reach one another over Bluetooth Low Energy, on a local network, and across the Internet from behind NAT, via rendezvous servers anyone can run. What madGLP requires of such a network, and what the network requires of the platform, has not been specified. We specify the networking layer beneath madGLP. Anything that can be done in GLP is done in GLP: the layer provides only what GLP cannot reach - the network stack, the location service, application attestation, and cryptographic primitives. Three transport underlays share one interface. Over PAN and LAN, an agent advertises a rotating recognition token derived from its key and time slot, so a peer who knows the key recognises it before contact and nobody else can track it; whether it answers unrecognised contacts is a per-underlay trust level set by GLP. Over WAN, a rendezvous server is a static-address host running the headless layer and a GLP rendezvous agent that coordinates hole punching, relays no payload, and belongs to no social graph. On every underlay, peers establish a mutually authenticated Noise session from Ed25519 keys, then attest, bound to the handshake hash, that each runs the application published under its developer's key, verified against Apple's and Google's roots with no third party contacted. One message protocol, over UDP datagrams and GATT writes, provides the fair, unordered, atomic and authenticated delivery madGLP assumes.

papers.title: Contextual Decision Making: Predictive or Generative
papers.abstract: Contextual decision making uses observed covariates to guide decisions under uncertainty. Two natural approaches are predict-then-optimize (PtO), which learns the conditional expected objective, and generate-then-optimize (GtO), which learns conditional uncertainty and optimizes using generated scenarios. We study when each approach is preferable by examining how the choice of learning target affects statistical accuracy and optimization tractability. Although PtO learns a narrower target, our regret bounds show how differences in smoothness can offset GtO's additional dimensional burden. Exploiting smoothness also raises an optimization tradeoff: within the class of nonnegative-weight PtO methods studied, a lower bound limits the gains from additional smoothness, while more flexible methods may introduce signed weights and lose the guarantee of preserving convexity. GtO preserves scenario-wise convexity, but requires learning a richer object and generating scenarios for optimization. Synthetic experiments and a real case study illustrate how these tradeoffs vary with data availability and problem structure. Together with the scope for reusing a model across tasks, our findings provide practical guidance for choosing between the approaches without identifying a universal winner.

papers.title: A note on the monotonicity of observational ergotropic advantage
papers.abstract: Very recently, Mahanti et al. (arXiv:2609.18735) introduced the observational ergotropic advantage, which gives the maximum value of extra work that a measurement can obtain with respect to all incoherent measurements. However, the above quantity does not show monotonic behaviour under the resource theory of measurement coherence. So, the search for a resource theory in which it is a monotone was open. We derive the monotonicity of this quantity using energy-preserving channels and passive resets as free operations and energy-incoherent measurements as free objects. We show the monotonicity property of the measure as a necessary criterion of measurement transformation, but it turns out not to be a sufficient condition. It is further established that the measure is not convex. A short analysis of bounds and tightness of the measure using a degenerate Hamiltonian is also given.

papers.title: OCTOPUS: Towards A Tag Model for Cross-Query Reuse in Semantic Query Processing
papers.abstract: Large language models make it possible to pose semantic questions over diverse, multi-modal data. Recent systems give such workloads the declarative feel of a database through semantic operators: relational operators whose conditions a model judges. Most of them now run on a relational engine, yet almost none keeps what the model says past the query: every judgment is discarded on completion and paid for again the next time a query needs it. We present the tag model and tag operators, the right unit for semantic processing, and OCTOPUS, a prototype built as a middleware over DBMS. Two mechanisms are central. First, the tag: each semantic answer a model produces is written back to the relation as data, which the database engine filters, indexes, and stores as it would any other. Second, the tag operator: the unit into which common semantic operators are translated, which fixes the granularity of reuse. A model judges a tuple once, and later queries reuse that judgment as data: through relationships between predicates, a stored judgment can accept a tuple for a later predicate, eliminate one that cannot satisfy it, simplify its test, or order the search of a query that stops early. On the movie scenario of SemBench, our prototype sends the model 10 to 108x fewer rows than iPDB, ThalamusDB, Palimpzest, and LOTUS at broadly competitive quality, and three of its eight queries issue no model call at all. More broadly, a database that keeps its judgments lets its schema grow from the questions its users ask, so that each semantic answer is paid for once, stays consistent across queries, and can be audited through its provenance.

papers.title: Geometry, Topology, and Confined Spectra Around Anisotropic Cosmic Strings
papers.abstract: We study scalar, Dirac, and electromagnetic test fields on a two-parameter family of static spacetimes, labeled by an angular winding number $k$ and an anisotropy parameter $α$ that shortens one direction of the transverse metric relative to the other. Only the members with $k=1$ and $α<1$ are conical, as for an ordinary straight cosmic string. The remaining members are nonconical and, except in the flat cases, curved and nonvacuum. A common spin-weighted connection Laplacian organizes the local equations, while the curvature coupling, global field conditions, and constraints are fixed separately for each physical field. Explicit frame transitions remove spurious winding dependence in the flat limit. For the nonconical members of the family, isothermal coordinates yield an exact factorization of the indicial equation and determine its monodromy: the indicial exponents are independent of the anisotropy parameter, although the finite-domain eigenvalues are not. We derive variational bounds and a weak-anisotropy selection rule for the scalar spectrum. The electromagnetic equations are obtained from the four-potential in Lorenz gauge, with gauge-invariant transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) reductions and an annular transverse-electromagnetic (TEM) mode. Finite-element computations on an annulus, validated against benchmarks, are consistent with the bounds, confirm the selection rule, give MIT bag Dirac and conducting-wall Maxwell spectra, and reproduce the invariance of the transverse-electromagnetic capacity under $k\mapsto2-k$, an exact consequence of a radial inversion of the Dirichlet energy.

papers.title: Minimal Alt(6)-modules with additive dimension on characteristic non 3
papers.abstract: We classify the minimal faithful Alt(6)-modules with an additive dimension in characteristic not 3. We also highlight the remaining work needed to complete the classification of minimal faithful Alt(n)- and Sym(n)-modules with an additive dimension

papers.title: Speculative Forking: Turning Idle Wait into Parallel Exploration for Repository Environment Setup
papers.abstract: Before developers can use a software project, they must first get it to run. This often requires installing the right language runtime, system packages, build tools, and test commands. Recent LLM-based agents automate environment setup by inspecting a repository, writing setup scripts, running them, and repairing the resulting errors. However, these agents still follow a sequential trial-and-error loop: they try one setup route, wait for slow commands to finish, observe the failure, and only then decide what to try next. Because environment commands often take long to run, this sequential workflow makes setup slow and limits exploration to one route at a time. We present SpecBuild, an LLM-based environment setup system designed to be both faster and more successful through speculative forking. SpecBuild explores candidate setup branches in parallel, returns the first committed environment, and discards the rest. It applies this design at two granularities: strategy-level forking explores alternative setup routes, such as different base images and dependency policies, while command-level forking predicts failures of running commands and prepares repair branches before those failures are observed. We evaluate SpecBuild on Multi-Docker-Eval, covering 334 tasks from 40 repositories and 9 programming languages. Across three backbone models, SpecBuild improves the success rate by 6.4 to 12.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline, while reducing average setup time by 22.4% to 41.6%. These results show that LLM-based environment setup need not trade speed for reliability: parallel speculative exploration can make agents both faster and more successful.

papers.title: Polarization Observations of NGC 315 with FAST
papers.abstract: We present new continuum and polarization observations of radio galaxy NGC 315 obtained with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) over 1.0-1.5 GHz. The FAST data detect diffuse large-scale polarized emission with a noise level of 0.065 mJy beam$^{-1}$ at resolution of $4'$. We derived a rotation measure (RM) map with an error of 1.1 rad m$^{-2}$ including systematic error. The intrinsic RM map was obtained after subtracting the Galactic foreground contribution. We estimated a total magnetic field strength of $\lesssim 1$ $μ$G across the source and a thermal electron density of $\sim 10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$ toward the northwest lobe. The fractional polarization analysis suggests a random magnetic-field component over a large area toward the northwest lobe.

papers.title: Numerical approximation of probabilistically strong solutions to the stochastic harmonic map heat flow
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic harmonic map heat flow into the sphere driven by a Stratonovich noise term that formally preserves the spherical constraint by construction. Starting from a fully discrete, implementable numerical scheme, we prove its convergence to the novel solution concept of probabilistically strong, analytically energy-variational solutions. This yields the first existence result for probabilistically strong solutions in the three-dimensional setting on the prescribed stochastic basis. In addition, we establish weak-strong uniqueness and illustrate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

papers.title: Affine and cyclotomic Brauer categorification via $\imath$-Kac--Moody $2$-categories: the integral type $\operatorname{AIII}$ case
papers.abstract: Continuing our work on the half-integral case, we construct generalized nilpotent $2$-representations of the integral quasi-split type $\operatorname{AIII}$ $\imath$-Kac--Moody $2$-category from affine Brauer actions with dot spectrum exactly $\mathbb Z$ on locally Schurian $\mathbb C$-linear categories. Conversely, nilpotent $2$-representations on such categories yield affine Brauer actions with spectrum contained in $\mathbb Z$. At the fixed vertex $0$, we directly define corrected generators and verify the nil-Brauer and mixed relations. For $\mathbf u$-admissible integral parameters at arbitrary positive level, we prove an isomorphism between the locally unital algebras of the cyclotomic Brauer category and a cyclotomic quotient of the principal $2$-representation. This gives compatible $\mathbb Z$-gradings on the category and its endomorphism algebras, providing a Brauer analogue of the graded realization of type $A$ cyclotomic Hecke algebras. Over algebraically closed fields of odd characteristic $p$, we also obtain both constructions with spectrum contained in $\mathbb F_p$, for the mixed affine datum restricted to its spectral weight subgroup.

papers.title: The limiting zero counting measure for Eisenstein series
papers.abstract: For an arbitrary congruence group $Γ$, we study the zeros of a generating set of the space of Eisenstein series of varying even weight for all $Γ(1)$-conjugates of $Γ$. These zeros form a $Γ(1)$-invariant set that descends to the modular orbifold $Y(1)$. It is known that, as the (even) weight tends to infinity, the set of zeros converges in the Hausdorff metric to finitely many geodesic segments. In this paper, we find the weak limit of the normalised counting measure of the zeros in the (natural) orbifold sense: if a geodesic occurring in the Hausdorff limit is parametrised by the unit circle $S^1$ via a Möbius transformation then the limit measure on this segment is the pullback of the Haar measure on $S^1$ by that transformation. For the proof, we first show a version of the Poincaré--Lelong theorem for orbifold curves, and then apply it on $Y(1)$ to reduce the problem to computing the scaled limit of the subharmonic functions $\log |E|$ associated to Eisenstein series $E$. This turns out to be the maximum of the negative logarithm of the modulus of finitely many linear functions supported on the relevant geodesic segments, and we finish the proof by showing that the associated measure has no atoms and making explicit, on each open segment, the distributional Laplacian of this function in terms of the argument measure. The non-atomicity allows us to conclude a sublinear growth rate in the weight for the total order of all Eisenstein series at a given point in $Y(1)$, and weak convergence also of the non-orbifold measure to the same limit.

papers.title: Multi-scale patterns arising from competing chemotactic interactions
papers.abstract: Classical chemotaxis models consider the directed motion of cells in response to a chemical gradient. Recent experiments suggest that biological microswimmers such as bacteria can perform chemotaxis toward multiple chemicals, which dynamically evolve depending on the distribution of the microswimmers. In this Letter, we consider a mass-conserving chemotaxis model in which pattern formation is driven by two competing chemicals, autoinducers and nutrients, where the former acts as an activator and the latter as an inhibitor for coarsening. We show that this can give rise to diverse patterns including long wavelength uninterrupted coarsening, Turing-like arrested coarsening, traveling waves as well as a novel class of mixed multi-scale oscillatory coarsening patterns, where a dense aggregate coexist with a dynamically spreading part of the population. We analytically derive the conditions for the onset of such patterns and discuss their physical implications, which significantly broadens our understanding of signaling active matter and pattern formation in general.

papers.title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
papers.abstract: The theory of Inflation, supplemented by fluctuations of the quantum vacuum, is the leading paradigm to explain the correlations of inhomogeneities at very large distances in the Universe. Particle physics methods fail when strong non-linearity and non-perturbativity are involved, leaving a whole landscape of untestable scenarios of inflation. Starobinsky's stochastic inflation can in principle treat inflationary inhomogeneities nonlinearly and classically as the Hubble radius becomes smaller than their wavelengths, but it was never formulated in full general relativity, which motivates this thesis. Using the Keldysh formalism of nonequilibrium quantum field theory, we first develop a validity criterion for the use of classical computations, and thus simulations, to probe inflationary interactions, finding analytically that the bispectrum can be extracted from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetimes. We then provide the first analytical solutions to the constraints for inhomogeneous initial conditions of numerical relativity simulations of inflation, and use them to explore its nonperturbative regime. Our main contribution is to obtain stochastic equations for the full set of inflaton equations in general relativity: this description incorporates the full nonlinear and backreacting evolution, is small-gauge-invariant, and is free of historical assumptions such as the gradient-free separate universe approximation. We implement these equations in the BSSN formulation of numerical relativity, demonstrating their correctness in slow-roll and ultra slow-roll scenarios via the satisfaction of the constraints, with a first look at eternal inflation. Finally, we extend our coarse-graining methods beyond General Relativity and single-field inflation, offering a phenomenological framework with the ambition of serving as a numerical particle collider for the early universe.

papers.title: Deformations of cohomology classes and spectral sequences
papers.abstract: We study spectral sequences as an obstruction theory to deforming cohomology classes via the Rees construction. A filtered complex is interpreted as an equivariant family over the affine line, in which higher spectral sequence differentials arise as obstructions to lifting cohomology classes through infinitesimal neighborhoods of the special fibre. This leads to various geometric and module-theoretic degeneration criteria. We give various applications to $\mathrm{Ext}$ spectral sequences for complex Lagrangians and the formality results of Melani-Rubió amongst others. For double complexes, we revisit the Khovanov-Qi decomposition on the Rees side and introduce a two-parameter Rees construction over the affine plane. The higher differentials of the two associated spectral sequences correspond to torsion modules supported on the thickened coordinate axes. We obtain degeneration criteria in terms of these modules and an intrinsic characterisation of the $\partial\bar\partial$-lemma.

papers.title: Political sense-making in "individual" human-technology-world relations: the case of LLM-generated autobiographies
papers.abstract: As AI systems increasingly mediate how people describe, recognize, and present themselves, their politics cannot be reduced to what remains hidden inside the "black box." This chapter argues that AI's political significance emerges within technologically, intersubjectively, and temporally mediated interpretive practices. Bringing Arendt's political philosophy into conversation with Gadamerian hermeneutics, the chapter develops a postphenomenological relational-temporal account of political sense-making across Human-Technology-World relations. Against the charge that postphenomenology remains individualistic and using the case of LLM-generated biographies, the chapter shows how seemingly private human-LLM encounters are worldly and collective. When users ask systems such as ChatGPT to describe them, they do not simply receive algorithmic representations. They interpret, contest, edit, share, and publicly test these descriptions. In doing so, people move interpretively among affective resonance, friction, public re-articulation, and the sedimentation of meaning. This means that the so-called "micro-level" of postphenomenological analysis is already saturated with publicity: affective uptake becomes communicable, reflection becomes accountable, and uses sediment into shared standards of appearance. Simultaneously, we show that once mediation is treated as relational and temporal, the political is not an add-on at the "macro" level; it is intrinsic to the very movement through which technologies amplify and reduce, stabilize and unsettle, and thereby compose a shared world in which judgment can take place. The chapter finishes by discussing several design and policy implications for AI of such political foregrounding in postphenomenology.

papers.title: The Compendium of Super-Quadratic Computational Quantum Advantages
papers.abstract: This compendium presents a structured collection of computational problems with credible prospects for realizing meaningful quantum advantage, focused on describing problem characteristics rather than specific algorithms. It is intended for non-quantum researchers and practitioners with strong computational backgrounds, particularly domain experts, seeking to assess the relevance of quantum methods to real-world problems. The compendium focuses on enumerating core problems for which there is good evidence that a quantum computer can realize more than a quadratic speedup in offline non-relativized time-complexity (e.g., as opposed to in oracular settings, streaming models, or communication advantages). Entries characterize the structural constraints that real-world instances must satisfy to realize those advantages in practice. The intention is to provide a reference that can be leveraged to connect quantum algorithms to practical use cases.

papers.title: OWLS: Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields for Zero-Shot Rover Navigation
papers.abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery. Project page: https://chahyon-ku.github.io/owls/

papers.title: Automated Multi-Line Bug Repair Using Model Checker Aided LLMs: A Case Study on RISC-V Processors
papers.abstract: Functional verification of Register-Transfer Level(RTL) designs has become a critical bottleneck in modern semiconductor development, often consuming the majority of project resources. Debugging, in particular, remains an especially time-consuming task, requiring careful analysis of simulation traces or counterexamples. Recent work has explored applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to RTL debug and repair with great promise. However, the existing approaches typically are for single-line bugs, operate in open-loop, rely heavily on prompts or retrieval, lack scalability, and often produce incorrect fixes. In this paper, we propose a novel automated RTL bug repair methodology that combines LLMs, assertions, and a model checker to provide scalable, trustworthy semantic grounding and formal guarantees. Concretely, the methodology leverages failing assertions to guide the LLM in generating patches for multi-line bugs. Each candidate patch is formally verified using a model checker (JasperGold), ensuring only valid repairs are accepted. We evaluate the efficacy and scalability of our methodology on the BRISC-V RISC-V core using mutation testing, introducing several mutation types, and demonstrate that our methodology can repair up to 98% of single-line RTL bugs and 93% of the multi-line bugs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show automated, LLM-assisted RTL multi-line bug repair results on a complex RISC-V processor design in a scalable manner.

papers.title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
papers.abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

papers.title: Gauge-field energy density in inflationary kinetic-coupling models: QFT regularization versus horizon cutoffs
papers.abstract: Coupling gauge fields to the inflaton can amplify their quantum fluctuations during inflation, with potential applications to a range of cosmological phenomena. A central challenge is to define finite and physically meaningful observables, such as the gauge-field energy density. In this work, we study an Abelian gauge field kinetically coupled to the inflaton through $f^2(φ)F_{μν}F^{μν}$ in a de Sitter background with $f\propto a^{γ_1}$, and compare conventional quantum-field-theoretic regularization with horizon-cutoff prescriptions. Using a hard physical-momentum cutoff and dimensional regularization, we derive the ultraviolet divergences in closed form and fix the remaining one-parameter finite-part ambiguity by requiring the coupling-induced total energy density to be nonnegative. We then examine five horizon-cutoff prescriptions based on characteristic scales of the mode equations. Their predictions depend sensitively on the choice of horizon scale and, for weak gauge-field production, can deviate substantially from the regularized result; for the adopted finite-part prescription, the minimal horizon agrees best with the regularized total energy density. As $|γ_1|\to 2$, where infrared modes dominate, the relative deviation of all prescriptions from the regularized result vanishes, independently of the finite-part prescription. Outside this regime, the separate electric and magnetic contributions, which can become negative after regularization, are not reliably reproduced by any of the horizon-cutoff prescriptions.

papers.title: New time-periodic solutions to the cubic conformal wave equation on $\mathbb{S}^{3}$: I Spherical symmetry
papers.abstract: We present a rigorous construction of novel time-periodic solutions to the radially symmetric cubic conformal wave equation on the Einstein cylinder $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^{3}$. Their existence, hinted by the earlier numerical studies (arXiv:2504.10513), complements prior results on Cantor sets of infinitesimally small solutions. Our proof, based on the contraction principle, requires extensive computations that are performed on a computer by the means of rational arithmetic. We are able to significantly reduce their amount by a thorough analysis of the inverse of the associated linear operator, leading to sharper analytical bounds, as well as introduction of simplified versions of certain relevant operators. We provide examples of three solutions with specific frequency; however, our techniques and tools can be directly adapted to prove the existence of other solutions conjectured in (arXiv:2504.10513).

papers.title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
